question.html:
Question 19
?

Find the gradient of the product f(x,y)g(x,y), given that f(x,y)=x+y,∇f(x,y)= i+ j,g(x,y)=ln⁡(x+y),∇g(x,y)=1x+y i+1x+y j.

a
(ln⁡(x+y)+1) i+(ln⁡(x+y)+1) j
b
(ln⁡(x+y)−1) i+(ln⁡(x+y)−1) j
c
(x+y) i+(x+y) j
d
(ln⁡(x+y)+1) j
e
ln⁡(x+y) i+ln⁡(x+y) j
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the product of two functions f(x,y) and g(x,y) is given by:

∇[fg]=g∇f+f∇g

So, using this product rule we obtain:

∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)]=g(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇g(x,y)=ln⁡(x+y)( i+ j)+(x+y)(1x+y i+1x+y j)=ln⁡(x+y) i+ln⁡(x+y) j+x+yx+y i+x+yx+y j=(ln⁡(x+y) i+ i)+(ln⁡(x+y) j+1 j)=(ln⁡(x+y)+1) i+(ln⁡(x+y)+1) j

last_observation.name: Question 19
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient
last_observation.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fg]=g\,∇\,f+f\,∇\,g
$$

So, using this product rule we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =g(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇g(x,y) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)(\text{ }i+\text{ }j)+(x+y)(\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }j) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }i+\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }j+\frac{x+y}{x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{x+y}{x+y}\text{ }j \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }i+\text{ }i)+(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }j+1\text{ }j) \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1)\text{ }i+(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1)\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 19
question.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)g(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =x+y,\, &  & ∇f(x,y)=\text{ }i+\text{ }j, &  &  \\ g(x,y) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y),\, &  & ∇g(x,y)=\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
question.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fg]=g\,∇\,f+f\,∇\,g
$$

So, using this product rule we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =g(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇g(x,y) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)(\text{ }i+\text{ }j)+(x+y)(\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }j) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }i+\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }j+\frac{x+y}{x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{x+y}{x+y}\text{ }j \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }i+\text{ }i)+(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }j+1\text{ }j) \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1)\text{ }i+(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1)\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 19
?

Find the gradient of the product f(x,y)g(x,y), given that f(x,y)=x+y,∇f(x,y)= i+ j,g(x,y)=ln⁡(x+y),∇g(x,y)=1x+y i+1x+y j.

a
(ln⁡(x+y)+1) i+(ln⁡(x+y)+1) j
b
(ln⁡(x+y)−1) i+(ln⁡(x+y)−1) j
c
(x+y) i+(x+y) j
d
(ln⁡(x+y)+1) j
e
ln⁡(x+y) i+ln⁡(x+y) j
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the product of two functions f(x,y) and g(x,y) is given by:

∇[fg]=g∇f+f∇g

So, using this product rule we obtain:

∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)]=g(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇g(x,y)=ln⁡(x+y)( i+ j)+(x+y)(1x+y i+1x+y j)=ln⁡(x+y) i+ln⁡(x+y) j+x+yx+y i+x+yx+y j=(ln⁡(x+y) i+ i)+(ln⁡(x+y) j+1 j)=(ln⁡(x+y)+1) i+(ln⁡(x+y)+1) j
question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient

solution.reasoning:
The product rule gives 
abla(fg)=g
abla f+f
abla g=\ln(x+y)(i+j)+(i+j), for x+y>0. Thus both components equal \ln(x+y)+1, matching option a. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key; the worked example concerns different functions.

feedback.name: Question 19
feedback.problem:
Find the gradient of the product $f(x,y)g(x,y),$ given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & =x+y,\, &  & ∇f(x,y)=\text{ }i+\text{ }j, &  &  \\ g(x,y) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y),\, &  & ∇g(x,y)=\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }j. &  & \end{aligned}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ is given by:

$$
∇[fg]=g\,∇\,f+f\,∇\,g
$$

So, using this product rule we obtain: 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)] & =g(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇g(x,y) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)(\text{ }i+\text{ }j)+(x+y)(\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{x+y}\text{ }j) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }i+\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }j+\frac{x+y}{x+y}\text{ }i+\frac{x+y}{x+y}\text{ }j \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }i+\text{ }i)+(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)\text{ }j+1\text{ }j) \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1)\text{ }i+(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)+1)\text{ }j\end{aligned}
$$

Question 19
?

Find the gradient of the product f(x,y)g(x,y), given that f(x,y)=x+y,∇f(x,y)= i+ j,g(x,y)=ln⁡(x+y),∇g(x,y)=1x+y i+1x+y j.

a
(ln⁡(x+y)+1) i+(ln⁡(x+y)+1) j
b
(ln⁡(x+y)−1) i+(ln⁡(x+y)−1) j
c
(x+y) i+(x+y) j
d
(ln⁡(x+y)+1) j
e
ln⁡(x+y) i+ln⁡(x+y) j
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the product of two functions f(x,y) and g(x,y) is given by:

∇[fg]=g∇f+f∇g

So, using this product rule we obtain:

∇[f(x,y)g(x,y)]=g(x,y)∇f(x,y)+f(x,y)∇g(x,y)=ln⁡(x+y)( i+ j)+(x+y)(1x+y i+1x+y j)=ln⁡(x+y) i+ln⁡(x+y) j+x+yx+y i+x+yx+y j=(ln⁡(x+y) i+ i)+(ln⁡(x+y) j+1 j)=(ln⁡(x+y)+1) i+(ln⁡(x+y)+1) j

question.name: Question 20
question.problem: What is the gradient of the product $f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)$ if $f(x,y,z)=xyz$ and $h(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)?$
question.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[fh]=f∇h+h∇f.
$$

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz)=yz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz)=xz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz)=xy\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\text{ }k=yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $h(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂h}{∂z}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)] & =f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z)+h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z) \\  & =xyz(\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =\frac{xyz}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{xyz}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{xyz}{z}\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 20
?

What is the gradient of the product f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z) if f(x,y,z)=xyz and h(x,y,z)=ln⁡(xyz)?

a
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))(x2 i+y2 j+z2 k)
b
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))(x i+y j+z k)
c
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))(i+j+k)
d
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))((y+z) i+(x+z) j+(x+y) k)
e
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))(yz i+xz j+xy k)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the product of two functions f(x,y) and h(x,y) is given by ∇[fh]=f∇h+h∇f.

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of f(x,y,z):

∂f∂x=∂∂x(xyz)=yz∂f∂y=∂∂y(xyz)=xz∂f∂z=∂∂z(xyz)=xy

Hence, ∇f(x,y,z)=∂f∂x i+∂f∂y j+∂f∂z k=yz i+xz j+xy k.

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of h(x,y,z):

∂h∂x=∂∂x(ln⁡(xyz))=1x∂h∂y=∂∂y(ln⁡(xyz))=1y∂h∂z=∂∂z(ln⁡(xyz))=1z

Therefore, ∇h(x,y,z)=∂h∂x i+∂h∂y j+∂h∂z k=1x i+1y j+1z k.

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain ∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)]=f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z)+h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z)=xyz(1x i+1y j+1z k)+ln⁡(xyz)(yz i+xz j+xy k)=xyzx i+xyzy j+xyzz k+ln⁡(xyz)(yz i+xz j+xy k)=yz i+xz j+xy k+ln⁡(xyz)(yz i+xz j+xy k)=(1+ln⁡(xyz))(yz i+xz j+xy k).

last_observation.name: Question 20
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating the Gradient Using the Properties of the Gradient
last_observation.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[fh]=f∇h+h∇f.
$$

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz)=yz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz)=xz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz)=xy\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\text{ }k=yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $h(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂h}{∂z}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)] & =f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z)+h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z) \\  & =xyz(\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =\frac{xyz}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{xyz}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{xyz}{z}\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k).\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 20
?

What is the gradient of the product f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z) if f(x,y,z)=xyz and h(x,y,z)=ln⁡(xyz)?

a
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))(x2 i+y2 j+z2 k)
b
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))(x i+y j+z k)
c
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))(i+j+k)
d
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))((y+z) i+(x+z) j+(x+y) k)
e
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))(yz i+xz j+xy k)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the product of two functions f(x,y) and h(x,y) is given by ∇[fh]=f∇h+h∇f.

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of f(x,y,z):

∂f∂x=∂∂x(xyz)=yz∂f∂y=∂∂y(xyz)=xz∂f∂z=∂∂z(xyz)=xy

Hence, ∇f(x,y,z)=∂f∂x i+∂f∂y j+∂f∂z k=yz i+xz j+xy k.

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of h(x,y,z):

∂h∂x=∂∂x(ln⁡(xyz))=1x∂h∂y=∂∂y(ln⁡(xyz))=1y∂h∂z=∂∂z(ln⁡(xyz))=1z

Therefore, ∇h(x,y,z)=∂h∂x i+∂h∂y j+∂h∂z k=1x i+1y j+1z k.

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain ∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)]=f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z)+h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z)=xyz(1x i+1y j+1z k)+ln⁡(xyz)(yz i+xz j+xy k)=xyzx i+xyzy j+xyzz k+ln⁡(xyz)(yz i+xz j+xy k)=yz i+xz j+xy k+ln⁡(xyz)(yz i+xz j+xy k)=(1+ln⁡(xyz))(yz i+xz j+xy k).

feedback.name: Question 20
feedback.problem: What is the gradient of the product $f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)$ if $f(x,y,z)=xyz$ and $h(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The gradient of the product of two functions $f(x,y)$ and $h(x,y)$ is given by

$$
∇[fh]=f∇h+h∇f.
$$

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of $f(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xyz)=yz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(xyz)=xz \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(xyz)=xy\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂f}{∂z}\text{ }k=yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of $h(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂h}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{x} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{y} \\ \frac{∂h}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))=\frac{1}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇h(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂h}{∂x}\text{ }i+\frac{∂h}{∂y}\text{ }j+\frac{∂h}{∂z}\text{ }k \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)] & =f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z)+h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z) \\  & =xyz(\frac{1}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{1}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{1}{z}\text{ }k)+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =\frac{xyz}{x}\text{ }i+\frac{xyz}{y}\text{ }j+\frac{xyz}{z}\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k) \\  & =(1+\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz))(yz\text{ }i+xz\text{ }j+xy\text{ }k).\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.html:
Question 20
?

What is the gradient of the product f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z) if f(x,y,z)=xyz and h(x,y,z)=ln⁡(xyz)?

a
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))(x2 i+y2 j+z2 k)
b
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))(x i+y j+z k)
c
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))(i+j+k)
d
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))((y+z) i+(x+z) j+(x+y) k)
e
 (1+ln⁡(xyz))(yz i+xz j+xy k)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The gradient of the product of two functions f(x,y) and h(x,y) is given by ∇[fh]=f∇h+h∇f.

Now, we calculate the partial derivatives of f(x,y,z):

∂f∂x=∂∂x(xyz)=yz∂f∂y=∂∂y(xyz)=xz∂f∂z=∂∂z(xyz)=xy

Hence, ∇f(x,y,z)=∂f∂x i+∂f∂y j+∂f∂z k=yz i+xz j+xy k.

Next, we calculate the partial derivatives of h(x,y,z):

∂h∂x=∂∂x(ln⁡(xyz))=1x∂h∂y=∂∂y(ln⁡(xyz))=1y∂h∂z=∂∂z(ln⁡(xyz))=1z

Therefore, ∇h(x,y,z)=∂h∂x i+∂h∂y j+∂h∂z k=1x i+1y j+1z k.

Finally, using the product rule, we obtain ∇[f(x,y,z)h(x,y,z)]=f(x,y,z)∇h(x,y,z)+h(x,y,z)∇f(x,y,z)=xyz(1x i+1y j+1z k)+ln⁡(xyz)(yz i+xz j+xy k)=xyzx i+xyzy j+xyzz k+ln⁡(xyz)(yz i+xz j+xy k)=yz i+xz j+xy k+ln⁡(xyz)(yz i+xz j+xy k)=(1+ln⁡(xyz))(yz i+xz j+xy k).

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Which of the following number lines represents the values of $w$ that satisfy $3w-7\le 5$ or $5w+7\ge -3$, or $2w<8?$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by solving $3w-7\le 5:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}3w-7 & \le 5 \\ 3w & \le 12 \\ w & \le 4\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14252742/assets/dfbf9fce10352e640bb62b75c49339e54c3d22b918e2dfb60a72472ef5129639.png)

Then, we solve $5w+7\ge -3:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}5w+7 & \ge -3 \\ 5w & \ge -10 \\ w & \ge -2\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14252742/assets/535934975bf21706e8bfa3b54fa51a0f344f585e89f3003ad042f6fb660c3441.png)

Finally, we solve $2w<8:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}2w & <8 \\ w & <4\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14252742/assets/ba806ca20f496c724c4411c282ab44d81d7713c7b8635b3c286faff1d7728f20.png)

To graph the values of $w$ that satisfy at least one of the inequalities, we overlay the three graphs on the same number line:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14252742/assets/f084c11e4faf4fdcfc69a32900bf62c1bddfa2266007f8f4ddecf8ab928230fa.png)

Therefore, the final solution is $-\infty <w<\infty .$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Find the set of values of $x$ that satisfy $-3\le 2x-7\le 1$ or $2+3x<2.$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by solving $-3\le 2x-7\le 1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-3 & \le 2x-7\le 1 \\ 4 & \le 2x\le 8 \\ 2 & \le x\le 4\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14252742/assets/909a1923438f6bf6931373c1a29cde24cd6ed08166c96769afa10a9a28696113.png)

Then, we solve $2+3x<2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2+3x & <2 \\ 3x & <0 \\ \frac{3x}{3} & <\frac{0}{3} \\ x & <0\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14252742/assets/daafda364f7c22d6db174e8fcc63092b754ca124854aa24a18bb7f0df024981c.png)

To graph the values of $x$ that satisfy either inequality, we overlay the two graphs on the same number line:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14252742/assets/b84ab4b3eeab7754193a0a41a2a1dc86338f7f0bed682b86b74fbe83cab6324d.png)

Therefore, the final solution is $x<0$ or $2\le x\le 4.$ We can write this using interval notation as $(-\infty ,0)\cup [2,4].$

question.problem: Find the set of values of $x$ that satisfy $-3\le 2x-7\le 1$ or $2+3x<2.$
question.worked_solution:
We start by solving $-3\le 2x-7\le 1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-3 & \le 2x-7\le 1 \\ 4 & \le 2x\le 8 \\ 2 & \le x\le 4\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14252742/assets/909a1923438f6bf6931373c1a29cde24cd6ed08166c96769afa10a9a28696113.png)

Then, we solve $2+3x<2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2+3x & <2 \\ 3x & <0 \\ \frac{3x}{3} & <\frac{0}{3} \\ x & <0\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14252742/assets/daafda364f7c22d6db174e8fcc63092b754ca124854aa24a18bb7f0df024981c.png)

To graph the values of $x$ that satisfy either inequality, we overlay the two graphs on the same number line:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14252742/assets/b84ab4b3eeab7754193a0a41a2a1dc86338f7f0bed682b86b74fbe83cab6324d.png)

Therefore, the final solution is $x<0$ or $2\le x\le 4.$ We can write this using interval notation as $(-\infty ,0)\cup [2,4].$

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
We start by solving $-3\le 2x-7\le 1:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-3 & \le 2x-7\le 1 \\ 4 & \le 2x\le 8 \\ 2 & \le x\le 4\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14252742/assets/909a1923438f6bf6931373c1a29cde24cd6ed08166c96769afa10a9a28696113.png)

Then, we solve $2+3x<2:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2+3x & <2 \\ 3x & <0 \\ \frac{3x}{3} & <\frac{0}{3} \\ x & <0\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14252742/assets/daafda364f7c22d6db174e8fcc63092b754ca124854aa24a18bb7f0df024981c.png)

To graph the values of $x$ that satisfy either inequality, we overlay the two graphs on the same number line:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14252742/assets/b84ab4b3eeab7754193a0a41a2a1dc86338f7f0bed682b86b74fbe83cab6324d.png)

Therefore, the final solution is $x<0$ or $2\le x\le 4.$ We can write this using interval notation as $(-\infty ,0)\cup [2,4].$

question.problem: What is the set of values of $x$ that satisfy $-2\le 2x-6\le 4$ or $12x-22<14?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14252742/assets/c82330c4ccd9aff01ac73cd1ebac56d50f685e0da258fb83ec619ebd11023694.png)

Therefore, the final solution is $x\le 5.$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: What is the set of values of $x$ that satisfy $-2\le 2x-6\le 4$ or $12x-22<14?$
question.worked_solution:
We start by solving $-2\le 2x-6\le 4:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & \le 2x-6\le 4 \\ 4 & \le 2x\le 10 \\ 2 & \le x\le 5\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14252742/assets/c82330c4ccd9aff01ac73cd1ebac56d50f685e0da258fb83ec619ebd11023694.png)

Then, we solve $12x-22<14:$

$$
\begin{aligned}12x-22 & <14 \\ 12x & <36 \\ x & <3\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14252742/assets/8ade78ec1b4adac7ee63d1eb3e5b5cc82ffe5b00437add005b7824dc2e0c05a9.png)

To graph the values of $x$ that satisfy either inequality, we overlay the two graphs on the same number line:

Therefore, the final solution is $x\le 5.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-0\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)=-3{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-3{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-3-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +8 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-2,\,-4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-4)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-4)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

2.Reducing a Quadratic Function Over the 2D-Space to the Canonical Form Using Orthogonal Transformations?

Given the quadratic form Q(x)=−3x12+2x1x2−3x22, find its canonical (diagonal) form yTDy and an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables.

M

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
questions.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=0.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
questions.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=0,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-2.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
questions.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-0\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 1
?

Given the quadratic form Q(x)=x12−4x1x2+4x22, find its canonical (diagonal) form yTDy and an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables.

a
D=[5000] and P=[−15252515]
b
D=[000−5] and P=[−213313313213]
c
D=[5000] and P=[−25151525]
d
D=[000−5] and P=[121212−12]
e
D=[5000] and P=[313−213213313]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[1−2−24]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|1−λ−2−24−λ|=0λ2−5λ=0λ=5,0

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=5, we have A−5I=[1−2−24]−5[1001]=[−4−2−2−1]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−5I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[−12]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=5, we get v1‖v1‖=15[−12].

  • For λ2=0, we have A−0I=[1−2−24]−0⋅[1001]=[1−2−24]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−0I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[21]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=5, we get v2‖v2‖=15[21].

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix D (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: D=[5000],P=[−15252515]

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-3-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +8 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-2,\,-4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-4)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-4)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)=-3{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-3{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-3-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +8 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-2,\,-4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-4)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-4)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 2
?

Given the quadratic form Q(x)=−3x12+2x1x2−3x22, find its canonical (diagonal) form yTDy and an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables.

a
D=[4002] and P=[−213313313213]
b
D=[−200−4] and P=[12−121212]
c
D=[200−4] and P=[313−213213313]
d
D=[−200−4] and P=[−25151525]
e
D=[400−2] and P=[12−121212]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[−311−3]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|−3−λ11−3−λ|=0λ2+6λ+8=0λ=−2,−4

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=−2, we have A−(−2)I=[−311−3]−(−2)[1001]=[−111−1]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−2)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[11]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=2, we get v1‖v1‖=12[11].

  • For λ2=−4, we have A−(−4)I=[−311−3]−(−4)[1001]=[1111]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−4)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−11]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get v2‖v2‖=12[−11].

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix D (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: D=[−200−4],P=[12−121212]

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=0.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=0,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-2.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix D, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are

λ1=2, λ2=0, and λ3=−2.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=2, we have A−2I=[−1101−10002]−2[100010001]=[−3101−30000]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−2I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[001]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=1, we get v1‖v1‖=11[001]=[001].

  • For λ2=0, we have A−0I=[−1101−10002]−0[100010001]=[−1101−10002]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−0I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[110]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get v2‖v2‖=12[110].

  • For λ3=−2, we have A−(−2)I=[−1101−10002]−(−2)[100010001]=[110110004]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−2)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v3=[−110]. Dividing v3 by its norm ‖v3‖=2, we get v3‖v3‖=12[−110].

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: P=[012−1201212100]

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

question.problem:

A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]

Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
question.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix D, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are

λ1=3, λ2=1, and λ3=−1.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: P=[00112−12012120]

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
question.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-0\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 1
?

Given the quadratic form Q(x)=x12−4x1x2+4x22, find its canonical (diagonal) form yTDy and an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables.

a
D=[5000] and P=[−15252515]
b
D=[000−5] and P=[−213313313213]
c
D=[5000] and P=[−25151525]
d
D=[000−5] and P=[121212−12]
e
D=[5000] and P=[313−213213313]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[1−2−24]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|1−λ−2−24−λ|=0λ2−5λ=0λ=5,0

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=5, we have A−5I=[1−2−24]−5[1001]=[−4−2−2−1]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−5I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[−12]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=5, we get v1‖v1‖=15[−12].

  • For λ2=0, we have A−0I=[1−2−24]−0⋅[1001]=[1−2−24]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−0I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[21]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=5, we get v2‖v2‖=15[21].

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix D (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: D=[5000],P=[−15252515]

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-0\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

feedback.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}-4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+4{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}1-\lambda  & -2 \\ -2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-5\lambda  & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-0\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

question.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)=-3{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-3{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
question.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-3-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +8 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-2,\,-4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-4)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-4)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 2
?

Given the quadratic form Q(x)=−3x12+2x1x2−3x22, find its canonical (diagonal) form yTDy and an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables.

a
D=[4002] and P=[−213313313213]
b
D=[−200−4] and P=[12−121212]
c
D=[200−4] and P=[313−213213313]
d
D=[−200−4] and P=[−25151525]
e
D=[400−2] and P=[12−121212]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[−311−3]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|−3−λ11−3−λ|=0λ2+6λ+8=0λ=−2,−4

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=−2, we have A−(−2)I=[−311−3]−(−2)[1001]=[−111−1]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−2)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[11]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=2, we get v1‖v1‖=12[11].

  • For λ2=−4, we have A−(−4)I=[−311−3]−(−4)[1001]=[1111]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−4)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−11]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get v2‖v2‖=12[−11].

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix D (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: D=[−200−4],P=[12−121212]

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-3-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +8 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-2,\,-4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-4)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-4)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

A=[−311−3]

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|−3−λ11−3−λ|=0λ2+6λ+8=0λ=−2,−4

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=−2, we have A−(−2)I=[−311−3]−(−2)[1001]=[−111−1]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−2)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[11]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=2, we get v1‖v1‖=12[11].

  • For λ2=−4, we have A−(−4)I=[−311−3]−(−4)[1001]=[1111]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−4)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−11]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get v2‖v2‖=12[−11].

feedback.problem: Given the quadratic form $Q(x)=-3{x}_{1}^{2}+2{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-3{x}_{2}^{2},$ find its canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables.
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we write down the matrix of our quadratic form:

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

To find the coefficients of the canonical form, we need to calculate the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-3-\lambda  & 1 \\ 1 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +8 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =-2,\,-4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-4,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-4)I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 1 & -3\end{aligned}]-(-4)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-4)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the diagonal matrix $D$ (writing the eigenvalues in descending order) and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
D=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 \\ 0 & -4\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
question.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=0.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

A=[1−10−110003],D=[300020000]

Consider the matrices given above. Find an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form Q(x)=xTAx to the canonical (diagonal) form yTDy.

a
[012−1210001212]
b
[−1212000112120]
c
[0−121201212100]
d
[013−1201312100]
e
[0−151210001512]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix D, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are

λ1=3, λ2=2, and λ3=0.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=3, we have A−3I=[1−10−110003]−3[100010001]=[−2−10−1−20000]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−3I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[001]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=1, we get v1‖v1‖=11[001]=[001].

  • For λ2=2, we have A−2I=[1−10−110003]−2[100010001]=[−1−10−1−10001]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−2I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−110]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get v2‖v2‖=12[−110].

  • For λ3=0, we have A−0I=[1−10−110003]−0[100010001]=[1−10−110003]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−0I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v3=[110]. Dividing v3 by its norm ‖v3‖=2, we get v3‖v3‖=12[110].

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: P=[0−121201212100]

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=0.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

question.problem:

Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$

A=[1−10−110003],D=[300020000]

Consider the matrices given above. Find an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form Q(x)=xTAx to the canonical (diagonal) form yTDy.

EXPLANATION

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix D, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are

λ1=3, λ2=2, and λ3=0.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=3, we have A−3I=[1−10−110003]−3[100010001]=[−2−10−1−20000]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−3I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[001]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=1, we get v1‖v1‖=11[001]=[001].

  • For λ2=2, we have A−2I=[1−10−110003]−2[100010001]=[−1−10−1−10001]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−2I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[−110]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get v2‖v2‖=12[−110].

  • For λ3=0, we have A−0I=[1−10−110003]−0[100010001]=[1−10−110003]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−0I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v3=[110]. Dividing v3 by its norm ‖v3‖=2, we get v3‖v3‖=12[110].

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: P=[0−121201212100]

solution.reasoning: The columns of P must be orthonormal eigenvectors of A in the eigenvalue order 3, 2, 0 specified by D. Option c has columns (0,0,1), (-1,1,0)/√2, and (1,1,0)/√2, respectively. These satisfy AP=PD and PᵀP=I, so PᵀAP=D and Q(Py)=3y₁²+2y₂². No Math Academy answer or grading evidence is provided.

feedback.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=2,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=0.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$
