question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
question.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=0,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-2.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 4
?

A=[−1101−10002],D=[20000000−2]

Consider the matrices given above. Find an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form Q(x)=xTAx to the canonical (diagonal) form yTDy.

a
[012−1201212100]
b
[012−2501215100]
c
[012−1210001212]
d
[−1201201012012]
e
[120−1201012012]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix D, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are

λ1=2, λ2=0, and λ3=−2.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=2, we have A−2I=[−1101−10002]−2[100010001]=[−3101−30000]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−2I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[001]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=1, we get v1‖v1‖=11[001]=[001].

  • For λ2=0, we have A−0I=[−1101−10002]−0[100010001]=[−1101−10002]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−0I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[110]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get v2‖v2‖=12[110].

  • For λ3=−2, we have A−(−2)I=[−1101−10002]−(−2)[100010001]=[110110004]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−2)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v3=[−110]. Dividing v3 by its norm ‖v3‖=2, we get v3‖v3‖=12[−110].

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: P=[012−1201212100]

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=0,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-2.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 4

A=[−1101−10002],D=[20000000−2]

Consider the matrices given above. Find an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form Q(x)=xTAx to the canonical (diagonal) form yTDy.

a
[012−1201212100]
b
[012−2501215100]
c
[012−1210001212]
d
[−1201201012012]
e
[120−1201012012]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix D, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are

λ1=2, λ2=0, and λ3=−2.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=2, we have A−2I=[−1101−10002]−2[100010001]=[−3101−30000]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−2I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[001]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=1, we get v1‖v1‖=11[001]=[001].

  • For λ2=0, we have A−0I=[−1101−10002]−0[100010001]=[−1101−10002]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−0I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[110]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get v2‖v2‖=12[110].

  • For λ3=−2, we have A−(−2)I=[−1101−10002]−(−2)[100010001]=[110110004]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−2)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v3=[−110]. Dividing v3 by its norm ‖v3‖=2, we get v3‖v3‖=12[−110].

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: P=[012−1201212100]

solution.reasoning: Option a has orthonormal columns (0,0,1), (1,1,0)/√2, and (-1,1,0)/√2, which are eigenvectors of A with eigenvalues 2, 0, and -2 in the order required by D. Therefore PᵀAP=D and Q(Py)=2y₁²-2y₃². The mathematics is certain, but no Math Academy answer or grading evidence is supplied.

feedback.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=2,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=0,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-2.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-2I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-2I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-2)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-2)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Question 5
?

A=[−100021012],D=[30001000−1]

Consider the matrices given above. Find an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form Q(x)=xTAx to the canonical (diagonal) form yTDy.

a
[−1212000112120]
b
[00115−25025150]
c
[012−1201212100]
d
[100015−2502515]
e
[00112−12012120]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix D, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are

λ1=3, λ2=1, and λ3=−1.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=3, we have A−3I=[−100021012]−3[100010001]=[−4000−1101−1]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−3I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[011]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=2, we get v1‖v1‖=12[011].

  • For λ2=1, we have A−I=[−100021012]−[100010001]=[−200011011]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[0−11]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get v2‖v2‖=12[0−11].

  • For λ3=−1, we have A−(−1)I=[−100021012]−(−1)[100010001]=[000031013]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−1)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v3=[100]. Dividing v3 by its norm ‖v3‖=1, we get v3‖v3‖=11[100]=[100].

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: P=[00112−12012120]

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above. Find an orthogonal matrix P such that x=Py defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form Q(x)=xTAx to the canonical (diagonal) form yTDy.

EXPLANATION

Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix D, we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix A are

λ1=3, λ2=1, and λ3=−1.

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of A.

  • For λ1=3, we have A−3I=[−100021012]−3[100010001]=[−4000−1101−1]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−3I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[011]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=2, we get v1‖v1‖=12[011].

  • For λ2=1, we have A−I=[−100021012]−[100010001]=[−200011011]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[0−11]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=2, we get v2‖v2‖=12[0−11].

  • For λ3=−1, we have A−(−1)I=[−100021012]−(−1)[100010001]=[000031013]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−(−1)I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v3=[100]. Dividing v3 by its norm ‖v3‖=1, we get v3‖v3‖=11[100]=[100].

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix P in the usual way, and this gives us the following: P=[00112−12012120]

solution.reasoning: Option e has orthonormal columns (0,1,1)/√2, (0,-1,1)/√2, and (1,0,0), which are eigenvectors of A with eigenvalues 3, 1, and -1 in the order specified by D. Hence PᵀAP=D and Q(Py)=3y₁²+y₂²-y₃². The mathematical answer is certain, but no Math Academy answer or grading evidence is supplied.

feedback.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices given above.
Find an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $x=Py$ defines the corresponding change of variables that reduces the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}^{T}\,Ax$ to the canonical (diagonal) form ${y}^{T}\,Dy.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Every quadratic form can be reduced to its canonical (diagonal) form using orthogonal transformations.

From the diagonal matrix $D,$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are 

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3,\,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=1,\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{3}=-1.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{3}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]-(-1)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{3}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{3}‖=1,$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{3}}{‖{v}_{3}‖}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, we construct the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following:

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 & 1 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: $\int -5{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
Factoring out the constant $-5$ and calculating the resulting integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -5{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =-5\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-5{e}^{x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Calculate $\int {(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3})}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\  & =0-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3})}+C=-\frac{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Calculate $\int {(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}\,\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8})}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡8 \\  & =0-\operatorname{ln}⁡8 \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡8.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8})}+C=-\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡8}+C\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Here, we combine the sum rule and our exponential rules to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int ({4}^{x}-{e}^{x})\,\text{d}x & =\int {4}^{x}\,\text{d}x-\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{4}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-{e}^{x}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Integrating an Exponential Function With a General Base
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\displaystyle \int -6(7^x) \, \textrm d x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we factor out the constant $-6.$ Then, we integrate the exponential function, and get

$$
\eqalign{
\int (-6)7^x  \, \textrm d x   
&= -6\int 7^x\,\textrm{d}x\
&=-6 \cdot \dfrac{7^x}{\ln 7} + C.
}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Integrating a Sum of Exponential Functions
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\displaystyle \int 5 \cdot 9^x +3 e^x \, \textrm d x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Here, we combine the sum rule and our exponential rules to get

$$
\eqalign{
\displaystyle \int 5 \cdot 9^x +3 e^x  \, \textrm d x &= \displaystyle 5\int 9^x \, \textrm{d}x+ 3 \displaystyle \int e^x \, \textrm{d}x\
&= 5\cdot \dfrac{9^x}{\ln 9} + 3 e^x +C.
}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Remember that the exponential function $e^x$ has the special property that the derivative of the exponential function is the exponential function itself. In other words, taking the derivative doesn't change anything, and we have

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm d x} \left(e^ x\right)  = e^ x.
$$

Since integration is the opposite of differentiation, and differentiating the exponential function leaves it unchanged, integrating the exponential function also leaves it unchanged. So, the integral of the exponential function is

$$
\displaystyle \int e^x \, \textrm d x = e^x +C.
$$

tutorials.name: Integrating an Exponential Function With a General Base
tutorials.problem:
Remember that if $a$ is a positive real number, then the derivative of $a^x$ is given by

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm d x}\left( a^ x\right)	=	a^ x \ln a.
$$

So, by "reversing" this process, we obtain the following formula for the integral of a general exponential function:

$$
\displaystyle \int  a^x \, \textrm d x  = \dfrac{a^ x }{\ln a} +C.
$$

For instance, suppose that we wish to calculate the integral 

$$
\int 2^x  \, \textrm d x
$$

To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\eqalign{
\int 2^x  \, \textrm d x   &= \dfrac{2^x}{\ln 2} + C
}
$$

tutorial.name: Integrating an Exponential Function With a General Base
tutorial.problem:
Remember that if $a$ is a positive real number, then the derivative of $a^x$ is given by

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm d x}\left( a^ x\right)	=	a^ x \ln a.
$$

So, by "reversing" this process, we obtain the following formula for the integral of a general exponential function:

$$
\displaystyle \int  a^x \, \textrm d x  = \dfrac{a^ x }{\ln a} +C.
$$

For instance, suppose that we wish to calculate the integral 

$$
\int 2^x  \, \textrm d x
$$

To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\eqalign{
\int 2^x  \, \textrm d x   &= \dfrac{2^x}{\ln 2} + C
}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Integrating an Exponential Function With a General Base
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3})}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\  & =0-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3})}+C=-\frac{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Question 3
?

Calculate ∫(13)xdx.

a
−(13)xln⁡3+C
b
ln⁡3(13)x+C
c
 (13)x3ln⁡3+C
d
 3(13)x+C
e
−3ln⁡3(13)x+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

∫(13)xdx=(13)xln⁡(13)+C

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

ln⁡(13)=ln⁡1−ln⁡3=0−ln⁡3=−ln⁡3.

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

(13)xln⁡(13)+C=−(13)xln⁡3+C

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Integrating an Exponential Function With a General Base
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8})}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡8 \\  & =0-\operatorname{ln}⁡8 \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡8.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8})}+C=-\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡8}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Calculate ∫(18)xdx.

a
 (18)xln⁡8+C
b
−(18)xln⁡8+C
c
 ln⁡xln⁡8+C
d
 −ln⁡x8x+C
e
 8xln⁡8+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

∫(18)xdx=(18)xln⁡(18)+C

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

ln⁡(18)=ln⁡1−ln⁡8=0−ln⁡8=−ln⁡8.

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

(18)xln⁡(18)+C=−(18)xln⁡8+C

\eqalign{
\displaystyle \int 5 \cdot 9^x +3 e^x  \, \textrm d x &= \displaystyle 5\int 9^x \, \textrm{d}x+ 3 \displaystyle \int e^x \, \textrm{d}x\
&= 5\cdot \dfrac{9^x}{\ln 9} + 3 e^x +C.
}
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Integrating a Sum of Exponential Functions
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Here, we combine the sum rule and our exponential rules to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (2{e}^{x}+{4}^{x}-2x)\,\text{d}x & =2\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x+\int {4}^{x}\,\text{d}x-2\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{e}^{x}+\frac{{4}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

∫(2ex+4x−2x)dx=

a
e2x+4xln⁡4−x2+C
b
e2x+x4ln⁡4−x2+C
c
e2x+x4ln⁡4−2x2+C
d
2ex+4xln⁡4−x22+C
e
2ex+4xln⁡4−x2+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Here, we combine the sum rule and our exponential rules to get

∫(2ex+4x−2x)dx=2∫exdx+∫4xdx−2∫xdx=2ex+4xln⁡4−x2+C.
question.knowledge_point: Integrating a Sum of Exponential Functions

observed_steps.name: Question 7
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Integrating a Sum of Exponential Functions
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Here, we combine the sum rule and our exponential rules to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int ({9}^{x}+3{e}^{x})\,\text{d}x & =\int {9}^{x}\,\text{d}x+3\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{9}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡9}+3{e}^{x}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

∫(9x+3ex)dx=

a
ln⁡99x+ex+C
b
x9ln⁡9−3ex+C

9xln⁡9+3ex+C

9ln⁡x+e3x+C

EXPLANATION

Here, we combine the sum rule and our exponential rules to get

∫(9x+3ex)dx=∫9xdx+3∫exdx=9xln⁡9+3ex+C.

judgments.reasoning: The earlier answer, option e, is correct because the derivative of -5e^x+C is -5e^x. Math Academy graded that submitted answer Correct, and its worked solution agrees.
The constant multiple rule gives (\pi/2)e^x+C, whose derivative is the integrand. The earlier answer, option d, was graded Correct, and Math Academy's worked solution states the same result.
The exponential integration rule gives (1/3)^x/\ln(1/3)+C. Since \ln(1/3)=-\ln 3, this equals option a. The earlier submitted answer was graded Correct and agrees with Math Academy's worked solution.
The exponential integration rule gives (1/8)^x/\ln(1/8)+C. Since \ln(1/8)=-\ln 8, this equals option b. The earlier submitted answer was graded Correct and agrees with Math Academy's worked solution.

Integrating term by term gives 4^x/\ln 4-e^x+C, option b, as previously answered and as Math Academy's worked solution states. The captured submission was instead option a and was graded Incorrect; that grade does not contradict the correct answer b.
Integrating term by term gives 2e^x+4^x/\ln 4-x^2+C, option e. Its derivative is the original integrand. The earlier submitted answer was graded Correct and matches Math Academy's worked solution.
Integrating term by term gives 9^x/\ln 9+3e^x+C, option c. Differentiation returns the original integrand. The earlier submitted answer was graded Correct and matches Math Academy's worked solution.

The integral is 6e^x+C by the constant multiple rule, and differentiating verifies it. Math Academy's worked solution explicitly states '=6e^x +C.', agreeing with the earlier mathematical answer. No learner grade or answer fields are supplied; the earlier response incorrectly added an answer field.

The constant multiple and exponential integration rules give -6\cdot 7^x/\ln 7+C, whose derivative is -6(7^x). Math Academy's worked solution agrees, stating: &=-6 \cdot \dfrac{7^x}{\ln 7} + C. No learner grade or answer fields are supplied.

Integrating term by term gives 5\cdot 9^x/\ln 9+3e^x+C, whose derivative is 5\cdot 9^x+3e^x. Math Academy's worked solution agrees, stating: &= 5\cdot \dfrac{9^x}{\ln 9} + 3 e^x +C. No learner grade or answer fields are supplied.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: $\int -5{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x=$
question.worked_solution:
Factoring out the constant $-5$ and calculating the resulting integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -5{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =-5\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-5{e}^{x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem: $\int \frac{\pi }{2}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x=$
feedback.worked_solution:
Factoring out the constant $\frac{\pi }{2}$ and calculating the resulting integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\pi }{2}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{\pi }{2}\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{\pi }{2}{e}^{x}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Calculate $\int {(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}\,\text{d}x.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3})}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\  & =0-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3})}+C=-\frac{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Calculate ∫(13)xdx.

a
−(13)xln⁡3+C
b
ln⁡3(13)x+C
c
 (13)x3ln⁡3+C
d
 3(13)x+C
e
−3ln⁡3(13)x+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

∫(13)xdx=(13)xln⁡(13)+C

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

ln⁡(13)=ln⁡1−ln⁡3=0−ln⁡3=−ln⁡3.

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

(13)xln⁡(13)+C=−(13)xln⁡3+C

last_observation.worked_solution:
To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3})}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\  & =0-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3})}+C=-\frac{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Calculate ∫(13)xdx.

a
−(13)xln⁡3+C
b
ln⁡3(13)x+C
c
 (13)x3ln⁡3+C
d
 3(13)x+C
e
−3ln⁡3(13)x+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

∫(13)xdx=(13)xln⁡(13)+C

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

ln⁡(13)=ln⁡1−ln⁡3=0−ln⁡3=−ln⁡3.

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

(13)xln⁡(13)+C=−(13)xln⁡3+C

feedback.problem: Calculate $\int {(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}\,\text{d}x.$
feedback.worked_solution:
To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3})}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\  & =0-\operatorname{ln}⁡3 \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{3})}+C=-\frac{{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+C\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Calculate $\int {(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}\,\text{d}x.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8})}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡8 \\  & =0-\operatorname{ln}⁡8 \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡8.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8})}+C=-\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡8}+C\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Integrating an Exponential Function With a General Base
last_observation.worked_solution:
To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8})}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡1-\operatorname{ln}⁡8 \\  & =0-\operatorname{ln}⁡8 \\  & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡8.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{1}{8})}+C=-\frac{{(\frac{1}{8})}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡8}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Calculate ∫(18)xdx.

a
 (18)xln⁡8+C
b
−(18)xln⁡8+C
c
 ln⁡xln⁡8+C
d
 −ln⁡x8x+C
e
 8xln⁡8+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

∫(18)xdx=(18)xln⁡(18)+C

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

ln⁡(18)=ln⁡1−ln⁡8=0−ln⁡8=−ln⁡8.

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

(18)xln⁡(18)+C=−(18)xln⁡8+C

Correct
EXPLANATION

To compute the integral of a general exponential function, we just need to divide by the natural logarithm of the base of the exponential function:

∫(18)xdx=(18)xln⁡(18)+C

Using the laws of logarithms, we have that

ln⁡(18)=ln⁡1−ln⁡8=0−ln⁡8=−ln⁡8.

So, we can simplify our final answer as follows:

(18)xln⁡(18)+C=−(18)xln⁡8+C

$$

2xln⁡x−4ex+C

4xln⁡4−ex+C

42xln⁡4−2ex+C

xln⁡4−ex+C

Here, we combine the sum rule and our exponential rules to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int ({4}^{x}-{e}^{x})\,\text{d}x & =\int {4}^{x}\,\text{d}x-\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{4}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-{e}^{x}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

∫(4x−ex)dx=

a
2xln⁡x−4ex+C
b
4xln⁡4−ex+C
c
42xln⁡4−2ex+C
d
−4xln⁡4−e2x+C
e
xln⁡4−ex+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Here, we combine the sum rule and our exponential rules to get

∫(4x−ex)dx=∫4xdx−∫exdx=4xln⁡4−ex+C.
question.knowledge_point: Integrating a Sum of Exponential Functions

solution.reasoning: Integrating term by term gives \int(4^x-e^x)\,dx=4^x/\ln 4-e^x+C, matching option b. Differentiation returns 4^x-e^x. The supplied example supports the method, but no Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.worked_solution:
Here, we combine the sum rule and our exponential rules to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int ({4}^{x}-{e}^{x})\,\text{d}x & =\int {4}^{x}\,\text{d}x-\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{4}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-{e}^{x}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
Here, we combine the sum rule and our exponential rules to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (2{e}^{x}+{4}^{x}-2x)\,\text{d}x & =2\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x+\int {4}^{x}\,\text{d}x-2\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{e}^{x}+\frac{{4}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

∫(2ex+4x−2x)dx=

a
e2x+4xln⁡4−x2+C
b
e2x+x4ln⁡4−x2+C
c
e2x+x4ln⁡4−2x2+C
d
2ex+4xln⁡4−x22+C
e
2ex+4xln⁡4−x2+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Here, we combine the sum rule and our exponential rules to get

∫(2ex+4x−2x)dx=2∫exdx+∫4xdx−2∫xdx=2ex+4xln⁡4−x2+C.

last_observation.name: Question 6
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Integrating a Sum of Exponential Functions
last_observation.worked_solution:
Here, we combine the sum rule and our exponential rules to get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (2{e}^{x}+{4}^{x}-2x)\,\text{d}x & =2\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x+\int {4}^{x}\,\text{d}x-2\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{e}^{x}+\frac{{4}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Integrating a Sum of Exponential Functions

solution.reasoning: Integrating term by term, 2e^x integrates to 2e^x, 4^x to 4^x/\ln 4, and -2x to -x^2. Thus option e is mathematically correct. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the example only supports the method.

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (2{e}^{x}+{4}^{x}-2x)\,\text{d}x & =2\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x+\int {4}^{x}\,\text{d}x-2\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{e}^{x}+\frac{{4}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡4}-{x}^{2}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

?

∫(9x+3ex)dx=

a
ln⁡99x+ex+C
b
x9ln⁡9−3ex+C
c
9xln⁡9+3ex+C
d
9ln⁡x+e3x+C
e
xln⁡9−3ex+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Here, we combine the sum rule and our exponential rules to get

∫(9x+3ex)dx=∫9xdx+3∫exdx=9xln⁡9+3ex+C.

feedback.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int ({9}^{x}+3{e}^{x})\,\text{d}x & =\int {9}^{x}\,\text{d}x+3\int {e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{9}^{x}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡9}+3{e}^{x}+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

∫(9x+3ex)dx=

a
ln⁡99x+ex+C
b
x9ln⁡9−3ex+C
c
9xln⁡9+3ex+C
d
9ln⁡x+e3x+C
e
xln⁡9−3ex+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Here, we combine the sum rule and our exponential rules to get

∫(9x+3ex)dx=∫9xdx+3∫exdx=9xln⁡9+3ex+C.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2},$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=9.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=9.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=9$ is the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=9.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{z}-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=4.$
questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=4.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {e}^{z}-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =4 \\ {e}^{z} & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4 \\ z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=4$ is the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4).$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)}{{e}^{x-y}},$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-2.$
questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=-2.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)}{{e}^{x-y}} & =-2 \\ z-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & =-2{e}^{x-y} \\ z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=-2$ is the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2{e}^{x-y}.$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-z-1},$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=1.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-z-1} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-z-1 & =0 \\ z & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=1$ is the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1.$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=12{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2},$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=12.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=12.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ 12{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2} & =12 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{6}-{z}^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=12$ is the hyperboloid of two sheets $\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{6}-{z}^{2}=-1.$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: Which of the following describes the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡z?$
questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-\operatorname{ln}⁡z & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡z & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-c \\ z & ={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-c}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get a family of curves:

$$
z={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-c},\,c\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: Which of the following describes the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)=-{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+z+3?$
questions.worked_solution:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ -{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}+z+3 & =c \\ z & ={x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}+c-3\end{aligned}
$$

If we let $c-3=C,$ we get a family of elliptic paraboloids:

$$
z={x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}+C,\,C\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)-\sqrt{xy}$ that passes through the point $P(1,1,e).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,e) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot e)-\sqrt{1\cdot 1}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=0.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)-\sqrt{xy} & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz) & =\sqrt{xy} \\ xyz & ={e}^{\sqrt{xy}} \\ z & =\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(1,1,e)$ is the surface $z=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{xy}.$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)=x-2y+z$ that passes through the point $P(1,1,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,-1) & =1-2(1)+(-1) \\  & =1-2-1 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=-2.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ x-2y+z & =-2 \\ x-2y+z+2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(1,1,-1)$ is the plane $x-2y+z+2=0.$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)=z-4{x}^{2}-6{y}^{2}$ that passes through the point $P(2,1,22).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,1,22) & =22-4(2)^{2}-6(1)^{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=0.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ z-4{x}^{2}-6{y}^{2} & =0 \\ z & =4{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(2,1,22)$ is the elliptic paraboloid $z=4{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}.$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{z}{y-x}$ that passes through the point $P(2,1,3).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,1,3) & =\frac{z}{y-x} \\  & =\frac{3}{1-2} \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=-3.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{z}{y-x} & =-3 \\ z & =-3(y-x) \\ z & =3x-3y \\ 3x-3y-z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(2,1,3)$ is the plane $3x-3y-z=0.$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{x-y+z-1}$ that passes through the point $P(1,1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,1) & ={e}^{1-1+1-1} \\  & ={e}^{0} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=1.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {e}^{x-y+z-1} & =1 \\ x-y+z-1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(1,1,1)$ is the plane $x-y+z-1=0.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Equation of a Level Surface
canonical_examples.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z) = x^2+4y^2-z,$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=0.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z) = c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c = 0.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}-z & =0 \\ z & ={x}^{2}+4{y}^{2} \\ z & ={x}^{2}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{1/4}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=0$ is the elliptic paraboloid $z = x^2+\dfrac{y^2}{{1/4}}.$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Level Surface

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Describing a Level Surface of a Function
canonical_examples.problem: Find the family of surfaces that describe the level surfaces of the function $f(x,y, z) = \ln(x^2 + 2y^2 - z^2).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & ={e}^{c} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{e}^{c}}+\frac{2{y}^{2}}{{e}^{c}}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{{e}^{c}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get a family of hyperboloids of one sheet:

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{e^c} + \dfrac{y^2}{e^c/2} - \dfrac{z^2}{e^c} =  1, \qquad c \in (-\infty,\infty)
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Describing a Level Surface of a Function

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding a Level Surface of a Function Passing Through a Point
canonical_examples.problem: Find the equation of the level surface for the function $f(x,y,z) = \sin{xyz}$ that passes through the point $P\left(\pi,1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
  f\left(\pi,1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&= \sin \left(\pi\cdot 1 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sin{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} = 1}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z) = c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c = 1.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡xyz & =1 \\ xyz & =\frac{\pi }{2}+2\pi k\end{aligned}
$$

where $k$ is any integer.

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P\left(\pi,1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is the surface $xyz= \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2\pi k,$ where $k$ is any integer.
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding a Level Surface of a Function Passing Through a Point

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Let's consider the following function: 

$$
w = f(x,y,z) =x^2 +y^2+z^2
$$

Sadly, it is impossible to plot this function because four spatial dimensions ($x,y,z,$ and $w$) are needed, and space as we know it is restricted to three dimensions. 

However, we can get an idea of how the function $f(x,y,z)$ behaves by plotting surfaces of the form

$$
\left\{(x,y,z)\in\mathbb R^3 \, : \,f(x,y,z)=c\right\},
$$

where $c$ is some value that is in the range of $f.$ These sets are called **level surfaces** because they can be visualized as surfaces in three-dimensional space, and are "level" in the sense that each surface corresponds to a constant value of $w.$

For this particular function, all level surfaces are spheres. For example, if we let $w = 4,$ we get

$$
x^2 +y^2+z^2 = 4,
$$

which is a sphere of radius $2$ centered at the origin.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14252753/assets/12de396a8460b929f656a44d701752e248180f926f22a5f5c3eeecf355e9f31a.png)

Functions with more than two input variables are sometimes called **hypersurfaces** because they can be thought of as surfaces that exist within a space whose dimension is greater than $3.$ For example, the function 

$$
w = x^2+y^2+z^2
$$

can be thought of as a sphere in four-dimensional space, and is sometimes called a **hypersphere.**

Another way of thinking about the level surfaces of this function is that they correspond to the intersection of the hypersphere $w=x^2+y^2+z^2$ and the **hyperplane** $w=c.$

Question 1
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=x2+y2+z2, find the equation of the level surface f(x,y,z)=9.

a
z2=3−x2+y2
b
x2+y2+z2=9
c
x2+y2+z2=3
d
z=3−x2−y2
e
z2=9+x2+y2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=9. So, we have:

f(x,y,z)=cx2+y2+z2=9

Therefore, the level surface for c=9 is the sphere x2+y2+z2=9.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Equation of a Level Surface
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=4.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {e}^{z}-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =4 \\ {e}^{z} & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4 \\ z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=4$ is the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4).$

question.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{z}-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=4.$
question.worked_solution:
The level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=4.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {e}^{z}-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =4 \\ {e}^{z} & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4 \\ z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=4$ is the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4).$

Question 3
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=z−ln⁡(x+y)ex−y, find the equation of the level surface f(x,y,z)=−2.

a
z=2ln⁡(x−y)+2ex+y
b
z=ln⁡(x+y)+2ex−y
c
z=2ln⁡(x+y)−2ex+y
d
z=ln⁡(x−y)−ex−y2
e
z=ln⁡(x+y)−2ex−y
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=−2. So, we have:

f(x,y,z)=cz−ln⁡(x+y)ex−y=−2z−ln⁡(x+y)=−2ex−yz=ln⁡(x+y)−2ex−y

Therefore, the level surface for c=−2 is the surface z=ln⁡(x+y)−2ex−y.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=1.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-z-1} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-z-1 & =0 \\ z & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=1$ is the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1.$

question.html:
Question 4
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=ex2+y2−z−1, find the equation of the level surface f(x,y,z)=1.

a
z=x2+y2−1
b
z=−x2−y2−2
c
z=−x2−y2+1
d
z=x2+y2−2
e
z=x2+y2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=1. So, we have f(x,y,z)=cex2+y2−z−1=1x2+y2−z−1=0z=x2+y2−1.

Therefore, the level surface for c=1 is the paraboloid z=x2+y2−1.
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Level Surface

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Equation of a Level Surface
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=12.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ 12{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2} & =12 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{6}-{z}^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=12$ is the hyperboloid of two sheets $\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{6}-{z}^{2}=-1.$

question.html:
Question 5
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=12z2−3x2−2y2, find the equation of the level surface f(x,y,z)=12.

a
x23−y24−z2=−1
b
x24+y26−z2=−1
c
x26+y24−z2=−1
d
x23+y26−z2=1
e
x24+y26−z2=1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=12. So, we have:

f(x,y,z)=c12z2−3x2−2y2=12x24+y26−z2=−1

Therefore, the level surface for c=12 is the hyperboloid of two sheets x24+y26−z2=−1.

observed_steps.name: Example: Describing a Level Surface of a Function
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Equation of a Level Surface
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-{z}^{2}) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-{z}^{2} & ={e}^{c} \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{{e}^{c}}+\frac{2{y}^{2}}{{e}^{c}}-\frac{{z}^{2}}{{e}^{c}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get a family of hyperboloids of one sheet:

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{e^c} + \dfrac{y^2}{e^c/2} - \dfrac{z^2}{e^c} =  1, \qquad c \in (-\infty,\infty)
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

Which of the following describes the level surfaces of the function f(x,y,z)=x2+y2−ln⁡z?

a
A family of paraboloids: z=x2+y2+c
b
A family of curves: z=ex2+y2+c
c
A family of curves: z=ex2+y2−c
d
A family of curves: z=ln⁡(x2+y2+c)
e
A family of hyperbolic paraboloids: z=x2−y2+c
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The level surfaces of the function f(x,y,z) are given by the following equation: f(x,y,z)=cx2+y2−ln⁡z=cln⁡z=x2+y2−cz=ex2+y2−c

Therefore, we get a family of curves: z=ex2+y2−c,c∈(−∞,∞)

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The level surfaces of the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the following equation:

$$

If we let $c-3=C,$ we get a family of elliptic paraboloids:

$$
z={x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}+C,\,C\in (-\infty ,\infty )
$$

question.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following describes the level surfaces of the function f(x,y,z)=−x2−3y2+z+3?

a
A family of elliptic cones: z2=x2+3y2+C
b
A family of elliptic paraboloids: z=x2+3y2+C
c
A family of hyperbolic paraboloids: z=x2−3y2+C
d
A family of elliptic paraboloids: z=−x2−3y2+C
e
A family of planes: z=x+3y+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The level surfaces of the function f(x,y,z) are given by the following equation: f(x,y,z)=c−x2−3y2+z+3=cz=x2+3y2+c−3

If we let c−3=C, we get a family of elliptic paraboloids: z=x2+3y2+C,C∈(−∞,∞)
question.knowledge_point: Describing a Level Surface of a Function

observed_steps.name: Example: Finding a Level Surface of a Function Passing Through a Point
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Describing a Level Surface of a Function
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
  f\left(\pi,1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&= \sin \left(\pi\cdot 1 \cdot \dfrac{1}{2} \right) = \sin{\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)} = 1}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z) = c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c = 1.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡xyz & =1 \\ xyz & =\frac{\pi }{2}+2\pi k\end{aligned}
$$

where $k$ is any integer.

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P\left(\pi,1,\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ is the surface $xyz= \dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2\pi k,$ where $k$ is any integer.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Level Surface of a Function Passing Through a Point
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,e) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1\cdot 1\cdot e)-\sqrt{1\cdot 1}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=0.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz)-\sqrt{xy} & =0 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz) & =\sqrt{xy} \\ xyz & ={e}^{\sqrt{xy}} \\ z & =\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(1,1,e)$ is the surface $z=\frac{{e}^{\sqrt{xy}}}{xy}.$

Question 8
?

Find the equation of the level surface for the function f(x,y,z)=ln⁡(xyz)−xy that passes through the point P(1,1,e).

a
z=exyxy
b
z=exyxy
c
z=exy2xy
d
z2=exyxy
e
z2=exyxy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the value of the function at P:

f(1,1,e)=ln⁡(1⋅1⋅e)−1⋅1=0

Recall that the level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=0. So, we have:

f(x,y,z)=cln⁡(xyz)−xy=0ln⁡(xyz)=xyxyz=exyz=exyxy

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point P(1,1,e) is the surface z=exyxy.

observed_steps.name: Question 9
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Level Surface of a Function Passing Through a Point
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1,-1) & =1-2(1)+(-1) \\  & =1-2-1 \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=-2.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ x-2y+z & =-2 \\ x-2y+z+2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(1,1,-1)$ is the plane $x-2y+z+2=0.$

Question 9
?

Find the equation of the level surface for the function f(x,y,z)=x−2y+z that passes through the point P(1,1,−1).

a
x−2y+z−1=0
b
x−2y+z+2=0
c
x−2y+z+4=0
d
x−2y+z=0
e
x−2y+z−3=0
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we find the value of the function at P: f(1,1,−1)=1−2(1)+(−1)=1−2−1=−2

Recall that the level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=−2. So, we have f(x,y,z)=cx−2y+z=−2x−2y+z+2=0.

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point P(1,1,−1) is the plane x−2y+z+2=0.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we find the value of the function at $P$:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,1,22) & =22-4(2)^{2}-6(1)^{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=0.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ z-4{x}^{2}-6{y}^{2} & =0 \\ z & =4{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(2,1,22)$ is the elliptic paraboloid $z=4{x}^{2}+6{y}^{2}.$

Question 10

Find the equation of the level surface for the function f(x,y,z)=z−4x2−6y2 that passes through the point P(2,1,22).

a
z=4x2+6y2+2
b
z=2x2+3y2
c
z=4x2+6y2−2
d
z=2x2+3y2−1
e
z=4x2+6y2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the value of the function at P:

f(2,1,22)=22−4(2)2−6(1)2=0

Recall that the level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=0. So, we have:

f(x,y,z)=cz−4x2−6y2=0z=4x2+6y2

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point P(2,1,22) is the elliptic paraboloid z=4x2+6y2.

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,1,3) & =\frac{z}{y-x} \\  & =\frac{3}{1-2} \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=-3.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{z}{y-x} & =-3 \\ z & =-3(y-x) \\ z & =3x-3y \\ 3x-3y-z & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point $P(2,1,3)$ is the plane $3x-3y-z=0.$

question.html:
Question 12
?

Find the equation of the level surface for the function f(x,y,z)=ex−y+z−1 that passes through the point P(1,1,1).

a
x−y+z−1=0
b
x−y+z=0
c
x−y+z−4=0
d
x−y+z+4=0
e
x−y+z+2=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find the value of the function at P: f(1,1,1)=e1−1+1−1=e0=1

Recall that the level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=1. So, we have f(x,y,z)=cex−y+z−1=1x−y+z−1=0.

Therefore, the level surface that passes through the point P(1,1,1) is the plane x−y+z−1=0.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2},$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=9.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=9.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =9\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=9$ is the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=9.$

question.html:
Question 1
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=x2+y2+z2, find the equation of the level surface f(x,y,z)=9.

a
z2=3−x2+y2
b
x2+y2+z2=9
c
x2+y2+z2=3
d
z=3−x2−y2
e
z2=9+x2+y2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=9. So, we have:

f(x,y,z)=cx2+y2+z2=9

Therefore, the level surface for c=9 is the sphere x2+y2+z2=9.

question.html:
Question 1
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=x2+y2+z2, find the equation of the level surface f(x,y,z)=9.

a
z2=3−x2+y2
b
x2+y2+z2=9
c
x2+y2+z2=3
d
z=3−x2−y2
e
z2=9+x2+y2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=9. So, we have:

f(x,y,z)=cx2+y2+z2=9

Therefore, the level surface for c=9 is the sphere x2+y2+z2=9.
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Level Surface

solution.reasoning: Setting f(x,y,z)=9 gives x^2+y^2+z^2=9, a sphere centered at the origin with radius 3. This is option b. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

feedback.worked_solution:

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =9\end{aligned}

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{z}-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2},$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=4.$
question.worked_solution:
The level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=4.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {e}^{z}-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =4 \\ {e}^{z} & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4 \\ z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=4$ is the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4).$

question.html:
Question 2
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=ez−x2−y2, find the equation of the level surface f(x,y,z)=4.

a
z=ln⁡(4−x2−y2)
b
z=4−ln⁡(x2+y2)
c
z=ln⁡(x2+y2+4)
d
z=4ln⁡(x2+y2)
e
 z=ln⁡(x2+y2)+4
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=4. So, we have f(x,y,z)=cez−x2−y2=4ez=x2+y2+4z=ln⁡(x2+y2+4).

Therefore, the level surface for c=4 is the surface z=ln⁡(x2+y2+4).

last_observation.worked_solution:
The level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=4.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {e}^{z}-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2} & =4 \\ {e}^{z} & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4 \\ z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=4$ is the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+4).$

question.html:
Question 2
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=ez−x2−y2, find the equation of the level surface f(x,y,z)=4.

a
z=ln⁡(4−x2−y2)
b
z=4−ln⁡(x2+y2)
c
z=ln⁡(x2+y2+4)
d
z=4ln⁡(x2+y2)
e
 z=ln⁡(x2+y2)+4
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=4. So, we have f(x,y,z)=cez−x2−y2=4ez=x2+y2+4z=ln⁡(x2+y2+4).

Therefore, the level surface for c=4 is the surface z=ln⁡(x2+y2+4).

solution.reasoning: Setting e^z-x^2-y^2=4 gives e^z=x^2+y^2+4, hence z=ln(x^2+y^2+4), option c. The logarithm's argument is always positive. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured.

z=4ln⁡(x2+y2)
e
 z=ln⁡(x2+y2)+4
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=4. So, we have f(x,y,z)=cez−x2−y2=4ez=x2+y2+4z=ln⁡(x2+y2+4).

Therefore, the level surface for c=4 is the surface z=ln⁡(x2+y2+4).

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)}{{e}^{x-y}},$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-2.$
question.worked_solution:
The level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=-2.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)}{{e}^{x-y}} & =-2 \\ z-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & =-2{e}^{x-y} \\ z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=-2$ is the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2{e}^{x-y}.$

question.html:
Question 3
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=z−ln⁡(x+y)ex−y, find the equation of the level surface f(x,y,z)=−2.

a
z=2ln⁡(x−y)+2ex+y
b
z=ln⁡(x+y)+2ex−y
c
z=2ln⁡(x+y)−2ex+y
d
z=ln⁡(x−y)−ex−y2
e
z=ln⁡(x+y)−2ex−y
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=−2. So, we have:

f(x,y,z)=cz−ln⁡(x+y)ex−y=−2z−ln⁡(x+y)=−2ex−yz=ln⁡(x+y)−2ex−y

Therefore, the level surface for c=−2 is the surface z=ln⁡(x+y)−2ex−y.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=-2.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)}{{e}^{x-y}} & =-2 \\ z-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & =-2{e}^{x-y} \\ z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=-2$ is the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2{e}^{x-y}.$

question.html:
Question 3
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=z−ln⁡(x+y)ex−y, find the equation of the level surface f(x,y,z)=−2.

a
z=2ln⁡(x−y)+2ex+y
b
z=ln⁡(x+y)+2ex−y
c
z=2ln⁡(x+y)−2ex+y
d
z=ln⁡(x−y)−ex−y2
e
z=ln⁡(x+y)−2ex−y
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=−2. So, we have:

f(x,y,z)=cz−ln⁡(x+y)ex−y=−2z−ln⁡(x+y)=−2ex−yz=ln⁡(x+y)−2ex−y

Therefore, the level surface for c=−2 is the surface z=ln⁡(x+y)−2ex−y.
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Equation of a Level Surface

solution.reasoning: Multiplying f(x,y,z)=-2 by the nonzero denominator e^{x-y} gives z-ln(x+y)=-2e^{x-y}. Thus z=ln(x+y)-2e^{x-y}, with x+y>0, matching option e. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)}{{e}^{x-y}},$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=-2.$
feedback.worked_solution:
The level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=-2.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ \frac{z-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)}{{e}^{x-y}} & =-2 \\ z-\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y) & =-2{e}^{x-y} \\ z & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2{e}^{x-y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=-2$ is the surface $z=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)-2{e}^{x-y}.$

Question 3
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=z−ln⁡(x+y)ex−y, find the equation of the level surface f(x,y,z)=−2.

a
z=2ln⁡(x−y)+2ex+y
b
z=ln⁡(x+y)+2ex−y
c
z=2ln⁡(x+y)−2ex+y
d
z=ln⁡(x−y)−ex−y2
e
z=ln⁡(x+y)−2ex−y
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=−2. So, we have:

f(x,y,z)=cz−ln⁡(x+y)ex−y=−2z−ln⁡(x+y)=−2ex−yz=ln⁡(x+y)−2ex−y

Therefore, the level surface for c=−2 is the surface z=ln⁡(x+y)−2ex−y.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)={e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-z-1},$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=1.$
question.worked_solution:
The level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=1.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-z-1} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-z-1 & =0 \\ z & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=1$ is the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1.$

a
z=x2+y2−1
b
z=−x2−y2−2
c
z=−x2−y2+1
d
z=x2+y2−2
e
z=x2+y2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=1. So, we have f(x,y,z)=cex2+y2−z−1=1x2+y2−z−1=0z=x2+y2−1.

last_observation.worked_solution:
The level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=1.$ So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ {e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-z-1} & =1 \\ {x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-z-1 & =0 \\ z & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=1$ is the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-1.$

question.html:
Question 4
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=ex2+y2−z−1, find the equation of the level surface f(x,y,z)=1.

a
z=x2+y2−1
b
z=−x2−y2−2
c
z=−x2−y2+1
d
z=x2+y2−2
e
z=x2+y2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=1. So, we have f(x,y,z)=cex2+y2−z−1=1x2+y2−z−1=0z=x2+y2−1.

Therefore, the level surface for c=1 is the paraboloid z=x2+y2−1.

solution.reasoning: For real u, e^u=1 exactly when u=0. Thus x^2+y^2-z-1=0, giving z=x^2+y^2-1, option a. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes this question's key.

Question 4
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=ex2+y2−z−1, find the equation of the level surface f(x,y,z)=1.

a
z=x2+y2−1
b
z=−x2−y2−2
c
z=−x2−y2+1
d
z=x2+y2−2
e
z=x2+y2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=1. So, we have f(x,y,z)=cex2+y2−z−1=1x2+y2−z−1=0z=x2+y2−1.

Therefore, the level surface for c=1 is the paraboloid z=x2+y2−1.

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=12{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2},$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=12.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=12.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ 12{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2} & =12 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{6}-{z}^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=12$ is the hyperboloid of two sheets $\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{6}-{z}^{2}=-1.$

question.html:
Question 5
?

For the function f(x,y,z)=12z2−3x2−2y2, find the equation of the level surface f(x,y,z)=12.

a
x23−y24−z2=−1
b
x24+y26−z2=−1
c
x26+y24−z2=−1
d
x23+y26−z2=1
e
x24+y26−z2=1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the level surfaces for the function f(x,y,z) are given by the equation f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in c=12. So, we have:

f(x,y,z)=c12z2−3x2−2y2=12x24+y26−z2=−1

Therefore, the level surface for c=12 is the hyperboloid of two sheets x24+y26−z2=−1.

Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.

In our case, we're interested in $c=12.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ 12{z}^{2}-3{x}^{2}-2{y}^{2} & =12 \\ \frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{6}-{z}^{2} & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=12$ is the hyperboloid of two sheets $\frac{{x}^{2}}{4}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{6}-{z}^{2}=-1.$
